## Key Terms

**Calculated field.** A field defined inside a PivotTable with a formula that uses other fields. Excel sums each field over the rows behind a cell and then applies the formula to those sums, so calculated fields suit ratios and differences of totals, such as margin percentages.

**Common-size statement.** A financial statement that expresses every line as a percentage of a base, such as net revenue for the income statement, so that its structure can be compared across periods or companies. Comparing lines within one period in this way is vertical analysis.

**Conditional aggregation.** Calculating a total, count, average, minimum, or maximum over only the rows that meet one or more criteria, as SUMIFS, COUNTIFS, AVERAGEIFS, MINIFS, and MAXIFS do.

**Control total.** A total calculated independently from a set of data, which the data must agree with, such as the sum of the invoice subtotals against the sum of the invoice lines. In a summary by category, the categories must add up to the control total, so a difference reveals a missing category, a duplicated row, or a formula that fails silently.

**Cost effect.** The part of a change in margin caused by a change in the cost of the same items. In a margin measured at standard cost, it is zero unless the standard costs themselves change.

**Cross-tabulation.** A summary of a measure across two dimensions at once, with one dimension in the rows and the other in the columns, such as revenue by product line and quarter. A PivotTable produces one.

**Drill-down.** Moving from a total to the parts or rows behind it, for example by double-clicking a value in a PivotTable or by adding a more detailed field to its Rows area.

**GETPIVOTDATA.** An Excel function that returns a value from a PivotTable by naming its value field and items rather than its cell address, so that the reference stays correct when the PivotTable's layout changes.

**Group By.** A Power Query command that summarizes the rows of a query by one or more columns, with aggregations such as sums and counts, before the result is loaded. It produces a trial balance from the ledger by grouping the entries by account.

**Histogram.** A chart of how the values of a measure are distributed, drawn as bars that count the values falling in each of a set of bins of equal width. It shows the shape of a distribution, such as a right skew.

**Margin bridge.** A decomposition of the change in margin between two periods into effects, such as volume, mix, price, and cost, that add up exactly to the change. It is often presented as a waterfall chart.

**Mean.** The arithmetic average of a set of values, their sum divided by their number, calculated in Excel with AVERAGE. A few very large or very small values pull it away from the typical value.

**Median.** The middle value of a set of values sorted in order, or the average of the two middle values when their number is even, calculated in Excel with MEDIAN. It is not affected by how extreme the largest or smallest values are.

**Mix effect.** The part of a change in margin caused by a shift in sales between items or products that earn different margins per unit, while the total number of units is held constant.

**Pivot cache.** The copy of the source data that a PivotTable summarizes. PivotTables built from the same source share it, with its calculated fields, and it updates only when the PivotTable is refreshed.

**PivotTable.** An interactive Excel summary built from a source table by placing its fields in the Rows, Columns, Values, and Filters areas. It calculates a value for every combination of row and column items, with totals, and it is updated by refreshing.

**Pre-closing trial balance.** A trial balance prepared at the end of a period before that period's closing entries, so that the revenue and expense accounts still hold the period's activity from which the income statement is prepared.

**Price effect.** The part of a change in margin caused by charging different prices for the same items, including changes in price-list reductions and promotional discounts.

**Show Values As.** A PivotTable setting that displays a value field as a share of a total, a difference from a base item, a running total, or a rank, without changing the values behind it.

**Skewed distribution.** A distribution whose values are not spread symmetrically around its center. In a distribution skewed to the right, the usual shape of accounting populations, a minority of large values pulls the mean above the median.

**Standard deviation.** A measure of how widely values are spread around their mean. In Excel, STDEV.S treats the values as a sample of a larger population, and STDEV.P treats them as the complete population.

**Substantive analytical procedure.** An analytical procedure that an auditor uses as evidence about whether an amount is misstated, by comparing the recorded amount with an expectation developed from plausible relationships and investigating differences above a threshold set in advance.

**Value field.** A field placed in the Values area of a PivotTable and summarized, by a calculation such as Sum, Count, or Average, for every cell of the PivotTable.

**Volume effect.** The part of a change in margin caused by selling more or fewer units in total, valued at the earlier period's margin per unit.

**Waterfall chart.** A chart that shows how a starting value becomes an ending value through a sequence of increases and decreases, with the starting and ending values drawn as totals.
